FAHLBUSCH, MD, and K. H. VOIGT, MD From the Sektion Elektronenmikroskopie, Labor fur Neuroendokrinologie, Abteilung Innere Medizin I der Universitdt Ulm, Ulm, West Germany, and Neurochirurgische Klinik, Klinikum Grosshadern, Universitdt Miunchen, Munich, West Germany precursor Transsphenoidally removed samples ofpituitary adenomas from 14 patients with Cushing's disease and 5 patients with Nelson's syndrome always contained groups of uniform small ACTHcells. Antibodies against the Pendorphin, proopiocortin ACTH, and 16kpeptide recognized material in typical adenoma cells.

A subpopulation of these cells, varying in number from sample to sample, specifically exhibited amelanotropin immunoreactivity. Most periadenomatous samples showed signs of severe degeneration. Typical Crooke cells only occurred in samples from patients with Cushing's syndrome, but, with this fragments exception, no clear differences between pituitaries of patients with Cushing's and Nelson's syndromes could be discerned.

Two other forms of ACTHimmunoreac- tive cells were observed: rare, single, highly immunoreactive cells, with characteristics of both normal and Crooke cells, and numerous syncytial groups of cells in an advanced state of disintegration, presumably the remnants of hyperplastic follicles. The four different corticotrophs are characterized according to their fine structure and immunoreactivity in this study. (Am J Pathol 1982, 106:332341) WHEN IT BECAME known that pituitary adrenocorticotropin (ACTH) is part of a large precursor glycoprotein also containing the amino acid sequences of the peptides Pendorphin, Plipotropin, amelanotropin (MSH), and a long Nterminal portion, the 16kfragment, 13 the peptide content of human pituitary adenomas in Cushing's disease was reexamined by immunologic methods.

Evidence has been presented that human adenoma cells synthesize the whole length of the proopiocortin precursor.47 As a consequence, Pendorphin immunoreactivity (IR) coexists with ACTH IR in adenoma cells,-"' the two peptides are secreted concomitantly in vitro,6''12 and plasma content in Pendorphin increases together with ACTH content in patients with Cushing's syndrome. 1316 We confirm some of these findings using antibodies against Pendorphin, ACTH and 16kfragment.

Moreover, specific aMSH IR was found in subpopulations of cells or in cellular granules in microadenomas of both Cushing and Nelson patients. Absence of circadian rhythm of ACTH release17 and poor suppression of plasma ACTH by glucocorticoids'8 may indicate an autonomous behavior of the adenomas. However, ACTH secretion in these patients can be suppressed by large doses of glucocorticoids"9 and stimulated by vasopressin administration20 and metopiron treatment.21 The differential behavior of adenoma cells and pituitary ACTHcells in response to adrenal factors is unclear.22 In the present structural and immunocytochemical examination of surgically removed microadenomas and periadenomatous pituitary samples, four different forms of ACTHcells are described.

A better knowledge of the cellular composition of periadenomatous pituitaries may be of prognostic value.26 Materials and Methods Subjects Adenomatous and periadenomatous tissue samples from pituitaries of 14 patients with Cushing's syndrome (all women, ages 14 to 60 years) and from 5 patients with Nelson's syndrome (3 women, ages 21, 36, and 40 years; 2 men, ages 36 and 57 years), were immersed in fixatives and processed for immunocytochemical and electronmicroscopic study immediately after removal by transsphenoidal surgery. The microadenomas measured on average 5 mm (310 mm) in diameter; the less compact periadenomatous samples had approximately equal volumes. About half of these tissue blocks were used for routine examination, the other samples for this study.
Fixation and Tissue Processing Fixative I was composed of 2% glutaraldehyde in 0.1 M phosphate buffer; Fixative II was Zamboni and De Martino's fluid." Fixation time was usually 24 hours.
The tissues were dehydrated in graded ethanol CORTICOTROPHS IN CUSHING'S DISEASE 333 and propylene oxide and embedded in Epon. No osmium was applied. Immunocytochemistry

The immunocytochemical procedures have been described in detail.2829 Semithin (0.5, u) plastic sections were attached by heat to glass slides and the resin was removed by Namethoxide.30 After being rinsed in phosphatebuffered saline (PBS: 0.01 M phosphate buffer, 0.9% NaCl, pH 7.3) and 10 minutes' incubation in swine normal serum (1:30 in PBS), primary antibodies raised in rabbits (Table 1) were applied overnight. The antibodies were visualized according to Sternberger et aWI by the following incubation steps: swine antirabbit immunoglobulins (from Dako, Copenhagen, Denmark), 1:100 in PBS, for 10 minutes; a short rinse in PBS; peroxidaseanti- peroxidase complex (from Dako), 1:50 in PBS, for 10 minutes; a rinse in Tris buffer; 3,3'-diaminobenzidine (from Sigma) 20 mg/100 ml Tris buffer, pH 7.6, with 7o/ 100 ml, for 10 minutes in the dark; a 250 Ml H202 rinse in H2O; dehydration and inclusion in Depex. The sections were examined and photographed with phase contrast optics and green filter, without counterstaining.

For localization of different antigens in the same cell, serial 0.5M-thick sections were incubated, each with a different antibody. An adenoma from a patient with Cushing's syndrome contained a subpopulation of aMSH cells and cells with a few single large aMSH immunoreactive granules. All microadenomas from the 14 patients with Cushing's disease and from 3 of the patients with Nelson's syndrome (all women) contained, at least in some area, clusters of uniform cells with marginal granules that were immunoreactive with antibodies against different proopiocortin fragments.

They surrounded erythrocyte-filled sinuses or touched the walls of blood capillaries with apparently closed endothelium that lacked fenestrae. Fine Structure and Immunoreactivity of Crooke Cells Typical Crooke cells were observed in periadenomatous tissue in about half the Cushing cases and in none of the 5 Nelson cases.

Crooke cells were much larger than adenoma cells (Figure 3a and c). Also, the hormonal granules had a larger average diameter than the granules of adenoma cells (360 ± 60 nm versus 276 ± 65 nm). Granules were often arranged in two circles: a perinuclear circle and a peripheral circle (Figure 3c and d).

The clear area between these circles contained some mitochondria and very few ribosomes, but extensive bundles of fine filaments (Figure 3e). Lysosomelike inclusions were frequent (Figure 3e). Crooke cells exhibited 16kfragment, aMSH, ACTH, and Pendorphin IR (Figure 4).

The much smaller adenoma cells differed from Crooke cells by many ribosomes and mitochondria, by absence of microfilaments and by scarcity of lysosomal inclusions. Both dense cells and syncytial follicles exhibited 16kfrag- ment, ACTH, Pendorphin, and some aMSH IR (Figure 4). The single, intensely immunoreactive dense cells resembled normal human ACTH cells most closely (Figures 4, 6, and 7). They contained large vacuoles (Figure 7a), like those described in normal corticotrophs.35

The numerous hormonal granules were spread over the whole cytoplasm (Figure 7a). In Zambonifixed samples many of the granules were decomposed, and their content was scattered in the cytoplasm (Figure 7c and d). These lytic granules occurred specifically in corticotrophs; granules from neighboring cells were not affected (Figure 7a and d).

Dense cells also contained bundles of filaments (Figure 7c). In our periadenomatous tissue samples dense cells were much less frequent than corticotrophs in normal human pituitaries. Syncytial follicles resembled hyperplastic cell accumulations.

They exhibited signs of advanced disintegration (Figure 8). Plasma membranes had disappeared, the less numerous granules were distributed irregularly over wide areas, and there were many lysosomal inclusions. The follicular material was contained in large bags of connective tissue.

Typically, syncytial follicles contained many nuclei and nuclear fragments of different sizes. In late stages of degenthe nuclear material appeared to have eration shrunken and was very opaque. In periadenomatous samples from both Cushing and Nelson patients syncytial follicles were most frequent and covered large areas of the sections (Figures 4 and 6).

Discussion The pituitary adenomas removed from 17 female patients with Cushing's or Nelson's disease contained, without exception, groups of small, uniform ACTH cells with the characteristics of actively synthesizing cells.

No structural differences were noted between adenoma cells from patients with Cushing's disease and those with Nelson's disease. In contrast to these cells, the adenoma cells from the two male patients were distinctly different. Antibodies that were raised against the proopio- cortin precursor fragments Pendorphin, ACTH, and 16kfragment recognized antigenic material in most of the typical adenoma cells.

Since these antibodies do not distinguish between the isolated sequence against which they were raised and this sequence as a portion of the precursor molecule, we do not know to what extent the peptides are stored in the cells as cleaved portions of the precursor. In serial sections distinct cells usually exhibited both aMSH and ACTH IR, but in some aMSH cells (Figure 2) ACTH IR was absent. These differences are presumably due to partial or complete conversion of ACTH into aMSH and the corticotropinlike intermediate lobe peptide (CLIP).37 Melanotropin sequences in this disease are likely to be produced and secreted in varying, often considerable amounts, although they may be absent in single cases. The main difficulty with the examination of periadenomatous samples is posed by the fact that we do not know how representative these tissue pieces are, in respect to the whole adenohypophyses of these pa- tients.

Only samples surrounding the microadenomas could be resected and examined. Therefore, the validity of quantitative statements is limited to small areas. We found that the great majority of the periadenomatous samples exhibited severe degenerative alterations.

Changes that must have developed some time before surgical removal consisted of masses of connective tissue, large blood sinuses, or accumulations of lysosomal inclusions in different types of hormonal cells. In periadenomatous tissue three different forms of ACTH cells were regularly observed. By structural criteria all three cellular forms were pathologic.

Crooke cells had typical wide hyaline areas occupied 340 MARTIN ET AL AJP * March 1982 by bundles of microfilaments, the number of ribosomes was reduced, and large lysosomes were present. Since Crooke cells have not been found after adrenalectomy (Nelson's syndrome), inhibition by high steroid levels due to ACTH overproduction by adenoma cells has been suggested as being responsible for the appearance of these cells.24'25 In our material, typical Crooke cells were absent in samples from patients who had been subjected to adrenalectomy.

Dense cells most closely resembled normal pituitary ACTH cells.3436 However, they were far less frequent than corticotrophs in normal pituitaries. Disintegration of granules, when treated with Zamboni's fixative, may indicate decomposition of granular membranes, and the occurrence of microfilaments in the cytoplasm is a characteristic that dense cells share with Crooke cells. The very large and numerous syncytial follicles were the most characteristic form of ACTH cell in periadenomatous tissue samples.

Accumulation of nuclear fragments indicated that these follicles were degenerated residues of hyperplastic, proliferating cells. At an advanced state of disintegration, hormonal granules were almost completely lost, and necrotic nuclear fragments were grouped together. Extensive impairment of corticotrophs by inhibiting factors or by degeneration correlates well with observed low plasma ACTHlevels over extended periods after surgical removal of microadenomas.9 Except typical Crooke cells, pituitary tissues from patients with Cushing's disease and those with Nelson's syndrome were indistinguishable.

In both kinds of samples, tissue disintegration prevailed, and dense cells and syncytial follicles were present. Thus, factors not necessarily of adrenal origin may be responsible for pathologic changes in pituitary corticotrophs.
